title: Paronychia (acute & chronic) and ingrowing toenail
summary: Acute paronychia is a painful bacterial nail-fold infection; chronic paronychia is an irritant, wet-work inflammation of the nail fold with loss of the cuticle, often colonised by *Candida*. Ingrowing toenail is a common, related problem.

glance.think: A red, swollen, tender nail fold: hours to days (acute) or weeks to months with a lost cuticle (chronic).
glance.engine: Acute: *S. aureus* or streptococci after minor trauma. Chronic: wet work and irritants break the cuticle seal, with *Candida* as a passenger or driver.
glance.backbone: Acute: warm soaks, drain pus, antibiotic only if spreading (flucloxacillin). Chronic: keep hands dry, cotton-under-rubber gloves, potent topical steroid ± topical azole.
glance.never_miss: Herpetic whitlow (do not incise), osteomyelitis or tendon sheath infection, and nail-unit melanoma or SCC presenting as ‘paronychia’.

what: **Paronychia** = inflammation of the proximal and/or lateral nail folds. **Acute** (<~6 weeks) is usually bacterial (*S. aureus*, streptococci, sometimes *Pseudomonas*) or herpetic whitlow; **chronic** (>~6 weeks) is often related to irritant dermatitis of the nail fold plus secondary **Candida** (and sometimes Gram-negative bacteria).

**Candidal nail disease** usually follows chronic paronychia: yeast involves the fold first, then may spread to the nail plate (onychomycosis / onycholysis). Tutor consensus for the Module 3 Week 2 Day 1 case: **candidal onychomycosis with paronychia** in a wet-work hairdresser with KOH yeast cells.

list: Repeated **wet work**, cold hands, manicure trauma, cuticle picking, and irritants lift/lose the cuticle → gap between fold and plate → colonisation by *Candida albicans* (± bacteria).
Occupations: hairdressers, cleaners, bartenders, food handlers, dairy/fishing, home wet work.
Host factors: hand dermatitis, diabetes, immunosuppression, poor peripheral circulation.

Candida nail-plate infection is **less common** than dermatophyte onychomycosis overall, and is relatively **more often fingernails** than toenails. Relevance of a positive Candida culture must be judged clinically (Candida can secondarily colonise dystrophic nails from psoriasis/trauma).

head: Feature
Typical findings
rows: Swollen, tender, erythematous proximal (± lateral) folds; **loss of cuticle**; fold lifted off plate; intermittent white/yellow/green discharge
Thickening, yellow/white/green/black discolouration, **transverse ridging**, onycholysis starting near the fold
Fingers (thumbs common); often **several** digits over time; wet-work hands
Hairdresser; 6 months yellow thumbnails; painful cuticles; yellow malodorous secretion; onycholysis; KOH **yeast**

features: Acute bacterial paronychia: rapid hours–days, usually **one** digit, marked pain, possible abscess — different tempo from chronic Candida-associated disease.

list: Clinical: chronicity, wet-work history, cuticle loss, multi-digit tendency, discharge.
**KOH / microscopy ± culture** of nail clippings and/or fold swab — yeast on KOH supports Candida; culture identifies species and co-pathogens.
Correlate lab with clinic: Candida in a dystrophic nail without fold disease may be secondary.
Consider bacterial swab if acute flare/abscess; viral swab if grouped vesicles (herpetic whitlow).

head: Look-alike
Distinguishing clues
rows: Hours–days; single digit; marked pain ± abscess; systemic signs if spreading
Grouped vesicles; severe pain; HSV history/exposure
Usually starts **distal/lateral**; toenails common; hyphae on KOH; ± tinea pedis
History of injury/footwear; mycology often negative

list: Keep hands **dry and warm**; cotton-lined waterproof gloves for wet work; change when damp.
Avoid cuticle cutting/picking and harsh manicures.
Emollient barrier frequently; trim nails short.
Occupational advice for hairdressers: PPE, dry between clients, treat hand dermatitis.

management: **Drug therapy (align with BNF/local formulary; confirm organism when possible):**

list: Chronic paronychia: treat **dermatitis of the fold** (short courses of topical corticosteroid ointment to the fold are often used in specialist pathways) **plus** topical antifungal/antiseptic solutions to the nail fold for weeks–months (e.g. imidazole solutions — check BNF).

Confirmed Candida nail/fold disease not settling: oral **itraconazole** or **fluconazole** (Candida-active). Tutor teaching for this case favoured **itraconazole** (broader spectrum vs Candida than terbinafine; fingernail regimens often ~6 weeks continuous or pulsed per product licence — **verify current BNF/SmPC**).
**Terbinafine** is first-line for many **dermatophyte** nail infections but is **less reliable** for Candida — do not default to it when yeast is the culprit.
Topical nail lacquers alone are often insufficient if matrix/proximal disease or significant fold infection.
Abscess: drainage pathway; antibiotics only when bacterial infection is clear.

management: **If no improvement after appropriate oral course:** revisit adherence, ongoing wet exposure, alternative diagnoses (psoriasis, trauma), re-mycology, and dermatology referral.

list: **No abscess:** **warm water (± saline) soaks 3–4 times a day for 10–15 min**, keep the finger dry between soaks, rest/elevate, and give analgesia. Most cases settle without antibiotics.

**Abscess (fluctuant, pointing pus):** **incision and drainage** (or lifting the eponychium with a blade) in primary care, minor injuries or urgent care. Partial nail removal if pus has tracked under the plate. Antibiotics are often not needed after adequate drainage.

**Antibiotics only if** there is spreading cellulitis, the patient is systemically unwell, or they are immunocompromised or diabetic: **flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily for 5–7 days**; **clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily** if penicillin-allergic (erythromycin in pregnancy); **co-amoxiclav** if from a finger-sucking child or a bite (anaerobes, *Eikenella*)

**Refer same day** for suspected **flexor tenosynovitis** (Kanavel signs: fusiform swelling, flexed posture, tenderness along the sheath, pain on passive extension), **felon** (pulp-space abscess), osteomyelitis, or spreading infection in diabetes.

**Recurrent acute episodes** in the same fold should make you think of an underlying chronic paronychia, an ingrowing nail, HSV, or (single digit, persistent, in an older adult) **SCC of the nail unit or amelanotic melanoma**.

**Causes:** cutting nails curved or too short, tight shoes, hyperhidrosis, a naturally involuted ("pincer") nail. Commonest in teenagers and young men. **Retinoids** (isotretinoin) and some EGFR inhibitors cause periungual granulation tissue that looks the same.
**Stages:** inflammation → infection with granulation tissue ("proud flesh") → chronic hypertrophy of the fold.

**Conservative care:** cut the nail straight across, wear wide-toe-box shoes, warm salt soaks, lift the edge (cotton wisp or dental floss), use a gutter splint. Topical antiseptic. Antibiotics only for spreading cellulitis.

**Definitive:** **partial nail avulsion with phenol matricectomy** by **podiatry**. Success is ~95% and lower recurrence than avulsion alone. Total avulsion is for recurrent or bilateral disease. Diabetes or PAD → **refer early to podiatry** (foot-protection service).

red_flags: Spreading cellulitis, lymphangitis, fever or a **tense swollen finger pulp** (felon) or tendon-sheath signs: same-day surgical assessment.
Grouped vesicles on the finger: **herpetic whitlow**, so do not incise.
Diabetes, peripheral arterial disease or immunosuppression with a toe infection: low threshold for referral.
A single nail with persistent ‘paronychia’, nail destruction or pigment: exclude **nail-unit melanoma or SCC**.
pearls: Treat the **fold environment**, not only the tablet — wet-work continuation is the common reason for “failed” antifungals (tutor follow-up question).
Warn about itraconazole/fluconazole **interactions** (CYP3A4), LFTs, pregnancy/contraception issues — counsel and check interactions software.
Nails grow slowly: cosmetic improvement lags mycological cure by months.

head: Post
Statement
Correction
rows: Chronic paronychia is caused by streptococci/*Pseudomonas*

**Chronic paronychia (>6 weeks)** is mainly an **irritant/eczematous** condition of the nail fold (wet work, cuticle loss) with **secondary *Candida* (± bacterial) colonisation**. Strep/staph cause **acute** paronychia, and *Pseudomonas* is a colonist (green nail). Treat with barrier repair: dry, gloves (cotton under rubber), emollient, **potent TCS ± topical azole** (CKS)
**Terbinafine is preferred for candidal paronychia/nail infection**

**Wrong for *Candida*.** Terbinafine is poorly active against yeasts and is the drug of choice for **dermatophyte** onychomycosis. *Candida* nail disease uses **itraconazole** pulses (or fluconazole off-label). Candidal paronychia without plate involvement uses a **topical azole ± TCS**
